slides.title:
I picked the thing
I had never heard of

rows.label: It was the one reference I could not picture
rows.text: A shipwreck, Shakespeare, a wave print — those I knew. “Glass flowers” sounded like decoration.

rows.label: They turn out to be scientific instruments
rows.text: Goodale wanted life-like teaching specimens because the alternatives were crude papier-mâché and wax.

rows.label: Fifty years spent defeating decay — then they modelled decay
rows.text: That contradiction is the reason this reference is in the novel.

rows.label: The personal connection
rows.text: Two broke students making something great in a borrowed apartment. So is finding the door locked.

slides.footnote: Then the research turned up two things I did not expect — slides 6 and 8.
slides.notes: About 60 seconds. Say plainly that you chose the unfamiliar option on purpose.

slides.title: A father, a son, and fifty years
paragraphs: Leopold Blaschka (1822–1895) and his son Rudolf (1857–1939) worked in Hosterwitz, near Dresden, from a line of jewellers and glassmakers reaching back to the **fifteenth century**. They first became known for glass models of sea creatures — jellyfish, squid, anemones — sold to museums with no way to display soft-bodied animals.

In 1886 Professor George Lincoln Goodale, founder of Harvard's Botanical Museum, commissioned a botanical collection. **Elizabeth C. Ware and her daughter Mary Lee Ware** financed it and gave it to Harvard as a memorial to Dr. Charles Eliot Ware, Class of 1834.

timeline.text: First models shipped — damaged in customs, still convincing
The most refined, most complex models
Leopold dies; Rudolf works on alone
Enamelled masterpieces — Red Maple, Oriental Planetree
Gallery reopens after a historic renovation

slides.notes: Land the sea-creature origin — it explains why they were already expert at translucency. Point at three dates only.

slides.title: Not blown. Built.
slides.intro: The Blaschkas used **lampworking** — glass tubes and rods softened in a flame and worked by hand at the bench. They made stems, leaves and petals separately, in batches, across many models at once, then assembled the finished plants.

steps.label: Wire armature
steps.text: Sections of glass tubing were strung onto wire like beads, giving projecting stems and leaves something to hold on to.

steps.label: Assembly, eight stages
steps.text: Tubes became stems; rods became leaves on wires; the two were joined and coloured; petals were pulled from rods, wired and coloured; corolla and calyx were formed last and strung on.

steps.label: Glue and gelatin
steps.text: Stamens and pistils were fixed with animal glue rendered from mammal hide. Raised leaf veins were built up in gelatin.

steps.label: Cotton for hair
steps.text: The furred leaves of the Common Mullein were made by blowing fine cotton flocking onto glue-tacky glass.

steps.label: Paint, then enamel
steps.text: Early models were cold-painted. After 1895 Rudolf brushed on coloured glass powders and fused them — hues nearly indistinguishable from a living plant.

slides.notes: Correct the assumption out loud: this is not glassblowing. Bench work with a flame, wire, glue and cotton — closer to jewellery than to a furnace.

slides.title: The novel gets the century wrong

left.label: what the novel says
paras: A German father-and-son team made them **around the turn of the nineteenth century**, as a commission from the university.
That would put the work around 1800. Leopold Blaschka would not be born for another twenty-two years.

right.label: what the record says
paras: Commissioned in **1886**, made from **1887 to 1936**. That is the turn of the twentieth century — and the family was Czech-German, not simply German.
Even Harvard's own pages give both 1886 and 1887 for the start, and both 780 and 847 species — depending on whether you count detail models.

slides.footnote: I am not presenting this as a mistake to catch the author out. It is a small error in a book obsessed with people who edit their own history — and it sits two paragraphs from Sam asking Sadie to misremember this exact day on his behalf. **The reader who checks gets rewarded.**
slides.notes: This is where the room wakes up. Take both panels slowly. Be fair — say you cannot prove intent.

slides.title:
A thesis statement
disguised as a field trip
paragraphs: The narrator asks how you preserve what cannot be preserved — how you stop time and death. Then, immediately: what is a video game about, if not the erasure of mortality?
slides.pull: That is the whole novel in one paragraph, and Zevin puts it in the founding scene on purpose.

rows.label: The title
rows.text: “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow” is Macbeth on how days pile up toward death. A game gives you that sentence with the ending removed.

rows.label: The mechanic
rows.text: Respawning is a glass flower. Ichigo dies and returns unmarked — endless immaculate tomorrows, free of the evidence of having lived.

rows.label: The character
rows.text: Sam's body is the opposite. It keeps the damage. His foot is rebuilt so many times a doctor tells him there is a limit.

rows.label: The closed door
rows.text: They never get in. The preservation machine is right there, locked, while the two mortal people make their promise outside.

slides.notes: The analytical core — slow down. If the class has not read Macbeth, give the one-line gloss.

slides.title:
The flowers that never
fade are fading
paragraphs: When Sadie visits in her mid-thirties, the blooms are not what move her. It is the Blaschkas' models of **decomposing fruit** — bruises and discolouration, held forever. Rudolf really did model diseased fruit into the 1930s.

panel.label: and the models themselves are deteriorating
bullets: Rudolf added lead to his enamels; in humidity the lead salts bloom to the surface as white crust.
Vibration flexes the parts until glass is lost and the inner wire corrodes.
The animal glues yellow, the gelatin veins lift, and soot from coal heaters had to be swabbed off.
A California Poppy lost a petal. It was replaced with pigmented acrylic resin — not glass.

after: So the object Zevin chose as her image of permanence is itself in conservation. Sam wants a body that does not keep the damage; the Glass Flowers keep it too. **Nothing is preserved. Some things are maintained.**
slides.pull: Her first instinct is to tell Sam. They are not speaking.
slides.notes: The slide nobody else will have. Deliver the conservation list quickly, then stop on “Nothing is preserved. Some things are maintained.” Pause.

slides.title: Three things, and one is the game's design

cards.title: The joke about the poster
cards.text: Sadie says it is pointless to advertise the Glass Flowers with a photograph, because the models already look real. If you do not know they are glass, the line is grumbling. If you do, it is her design philosophy: an imitation good enough stops being an imitation.

cards.title: The woman in the gallery
cards.text: An elderly visitor walks the whole exhibit, then asks Sadie where the glass flowers are. She thought she had been looking at real ones. That is the payoff of a fifty-year project — and the effect Sadie chases when she styles the game after a woodblock print.

cards.title: Why a closed museum matters
cards.text: Sam stages his proposal at a monument to permanence and is locked out of it. Their partnership begins with an absence he later asks to have written out of the record. Knowing what is behind that door turns the scene into an omen, not an anecdote.

slides.footnote: A reader who skims past “Glass Flowers” still follows the plot. What they lose is **the reason Ichigo looks the way it does** — Sadie's rule that you make the limitation part of the style, that a convincing surface beats an accurate one.
slides.notes: Three beats, not one block. Say the words “what would be lost is…”

slides.title: Ninety seconds at the lamp
paragraphs: Harvard's **From the Hands of the Makers** includes a demonstration filmed at the Corning Museum of Glass on a nineteenth-century wooden lampworking table — the same kind of bench the Blaschkas used.
Watch what the hands are doing: the flame is small, the glass is worked slowly, and every part is made one at a time.
slides.note: Play 1:30 maximum — the assignment caps video at two minutes.
slides.notes: Needs internet. Click play, run about ninety seconds, stop it yourself. If the embed fails, use a browser tab you loaded before class.

slides.title:
Sam asked for
the story to be
told wrong
paragraphs: He wanted the version where the exhibit was open — where two people decided to build worlds inside a room that had already defeated death. Sadie tells it the other way, and calls telling it truthfully a small betrayal of him.

Games, glass models and the stories we tell about ourselves are all attempts to hold something still. None of them stop the thing they were built to stop — they only buy time, and someone has to keep paying for it. **The Blaschkas' most affecting work was never the perfect bloom. It was the rotting apple, kept.**
slides.notes: Land on “the rotting apple, kept.” Stop talking — the line is the summary.
